instagram_reel.hook: This is how wine gets that creamy, luxe feel — and it’s not oak.
instagram_reel.script:
Okay, wine word of the day: lees. After fermentation, the yeast is done doing its job and settles at the bottom of the tank or barrel. That sediment is called lees. 

If a winemaker leaves the wine sitting with those lees, that’s lees aging — or sur lie. And yes, it can make a wine feel creamier, rounder, and a little more luxe on the palate.

It’s especially great for high-acid whites and sparkling wines, because it adds texture without making the wine heavy. Think more polish, more depth, more interest.

So if a wine tastes a little more silky or bready than you expected, lees might be the reason.

linkedin.post:
Lees aging is one of the most useful tools in a winemaker’s toolkit because it does more than add complexity — it changes texture.

After fermentation, the spent yeast cells and sediment left behind are called lees. When wine remains in contact with those lees, the process known as sur lie aging can bring added creaminess, body, and depth.

That’s why it shows up so often in high-acid white wines and traditional-method sparkling wines. The goal isn’t weight for weight’s sake. It’s balance, polish, and a more complete palate experience.

From a production standpoint, lees can also help protect wine from oxidation and support stability. That makes this a practical choice as much as a stylistic one.

When done well, lees aging is a quiet flex: not flashy, just effective. It’s one of those techniques that turns good wine into something memorable.
